title: Playful Banter
tagline: Tease like a friend, never like a bully.
description: Friendly roasting, quick comebacks and laughing at yourself. How to trade jokes with friends and travellers, lose a round gracefully, and notice when the teasing should stop.

vibe.scenario: A friend grins: "You're late again. Did you walk here from Kathmandu?"

options.text: I took the scenic route. Through three momo shops.
At least I'm not always broke like you, borrowing money from everyone every week.

vibe.why: Accept the tease and make it bigger. Hitting back with something real turns a game into a fight.

vibe.scenario: A traveller beats you and celebrates loudly.

options.text: Enjoy it. I let you win so you'd have a nice memory of Nepal.
You only won because the board is bad. And you cheated twice, I saw it.

vibe.why: A playful excuse shows you don't take it seriously. Being a good loser is very attractive.

vibe.scenario: A friend looks at your new haircut: "Did your barber fall asleep?"

options.text: Haha, maybe. I don't know, I just told him to cut it short, and this is what happened.
He did. I'm calling it "monsoon style" — nobody knows what's coming.

vibe.why: Laughing at yourself first takes all the power out of the tease — and makes everyone like you more.

vibe.scenario: A friend makes a joke about a traveller's weight. The traveller goes quiet.

options.text: Okay, that one missed. Anyway — who wants the last momo? Not me, I'm being noble.

vibe.why: Name it lightly, then move the attention. You protect the traveller without starting a fight.

vibe.scenario: A friend rolls their eyes: "You think you're so charming."

options.text: Think? I have a certificate. It's from my mother, but still.
No, I don't. I'm just a normal person, I'm just being friendly, that's all, really.

vibe.why: A big claim followed by a small, silly detail is the classic banter rhythm.

vibe.scenario: A British traveller laughs: "Where did you learn the word 'splendid'? From the Queen?"

options.text: My English is better than yours.
From old British trekkers. They tipped in words instead of money.
From movies, mostly. And from my English teacher at school. She liked old British words.

vibe.why: A gentle joke about their country, in their style. They'll laugh, because it's the kind of joke they make.

vibe.scenario: Your traveller friend got badly sunburnt on the boat.

options.text: Ha! You look terrible, you should see yourself — everyone is laughing at you.
You look like a very handsome tomato. The pharmacy has aloe vera — I'll walk you.

vibe.why: The tease is soft, and the offer shows you care. That combination is what real friends do.

vibe.scenario: A traveller announces, "I'm the best dancer here."

options.text: Okay, show us, then. Let's see. Go on. Everybody's watching now, so you have to dance.
Bold claim. The floor is yours — we're the judges, and we're very harsh.

vibe.why: Turn their brag into a show. Everyone gets to have fun, including them.

vibe.scenario: You ordered for the whole table and got it completely wrong. Your friends are laughing.

options.text: It's the waiter's fault. He didn't listen properly to what I said.
In my defence, I was very confident. Confidence is half the job. The other half is being right.

vibe.why: When you're the joke, join in. It shows confidence, and the moment passes with a laugh.

vibe.scenario: A traveller hits you with a brilliant comeback. They clearly won that round.

options.text: Okay, that was good. I'm writing that down. You win this round.
Haha. Okay. Yeah. That was a good one, I guess. Fine. You got me there.

vibe.why: Praising a good comeback makes the game fun for both of you. People love someone who can lose with a smile.

vibe.scenario: Your friend just went through a painful breakup. The group starts teasing him like usual.

options.text: Come on, cheer up! She wasn't that great anyway, ha!
Let's pick on someone who can take it tonight — me. Go on, do my haircut again.

vibe.why: You protected him without making it awkward, by offering yourself as the target.

vibe.scenario: A tourist jokes, "Nothing in Nepal ever starts on time!"

options.text: We're not late. We're on mountain time — more relaxed, better views.
Your country has problems too, you know. Big ones.

vibe.why: Agree with the fact, change the story. National pride works best with a smile.

cards.text: I'm not bad, I'm generous. I'm letting you feel good about yourself.
cards.why: Flips the tease with a smile.

cards.text: Dangerous is exciting. Second plate, or are you scared?
cards.why: Accepts the label and dares them.

cards.text: Once, last year. It was awful. Never again.
cards.why: A short, silly answer that invites more play.
Now it feels like a real criticism.

cards.text: Only because I finally found someone worth talking to. Also, I've had four teas.
cards.why: A compliment and an excuse, both funny.

cards.text: Great — tell me your best joke, and I'll pretend to laugh.
cards.why: Accepts the challenge and hands them the stage.

yesAnd.prompt: Your motorbike is older than me.

cards.text: And it's still faster than you up the hill. Respect your elders.
cards.why: Defends the bike with a joke back at them.

yesAnd.prompt: You're such a tour guide — always giving advice.

cards.text: Occupational hazard. Free advice: order the chocolate cake.
cards.why: Owns it and immediately does it again, which is the joke.
Takes a friendly tease as a complaint.

yesAnd.pattern: Own it and do it again

cards.text: Then I'll sing it myself. Is that better or worse?
cards.why: Makes the threat funnier and asks them to choose.

upgrader.clunky: Haha, you are very, very bad at this game, very bad.
upgrader.why: A tease that pretends to comfort is funnier than a direct insult.

upgrader.clunky: Sorry, sorry, I was joking, I didn't mean, sorry.
upgrader.why: When a joke hurts, own it cleanly. "I was joking" puts the blame on them for not laughing.

upgrader.clunky: You are always late, always, every time late, always.
upgrader.why: Exaggeration makes a complaint into a joke. Repetition just makes it a complaint.

upgrader.clunky: I am not a good dancer, I am very bad, so bad.
distractors: I am not a good dancer
upgrader.why: Take a famous phrase and add a twist at the end. Self-deprecation with a punchline.

upgrader.clunky: Your joke is not funny, I don't like, not funny.
upgrader.why: Playful mercy is funnier than a flat "not funny". It keeps the game going.

upgrader.clunky: You won, okay, you are better, okay, fine, you won.
upgrader.why: Admit defeat, then promise a rematch. That's losing with style.

dropIn.fact: Psychologist Robert Provine found that people are about 30 times more likely to laugh when they're with others than when they're alone.
dropIn.source: Robert R. Provine, "Laughter: A Scientific Investigation" (2000)
dropIn.prompt: A friend asks, "Why do we laugh so much more when we're together?"

options.why: You do know, and it's a great fact.

options.text: Laughing is mostly social — one researcher found we laugh about thirty times more with other people. So really, you owe me for all this.
options.why: The fact, plus a cheeky tag that proves the point.

options.text: Research says we laugh about 30 times more with other people.

dropIn.fact: When Provine studied real conversations, he found most laughter came after ordinary comments — not after jokes.
dropIn.source: Robert R. Provine, "Laughter: A Scientific Investigation" (2000)
dropIn.prompt: A friend sighs, "I'm just not funny. I don't know any jokes."

options.why: Misses the point of the research.

options.text: Most laughter in conversation isn't about jokes. It usually comes after normal things people say, like "see you later" or "where are you going?", and things like that.
options.why: True and detailed, but it never gets round to comforting your friend.

options.text: You don't need jokes. A researcher who listened to real conversations found most laughter comes after normal sentences. Just relax and play.

dropIn.fact: Psychologists describe different humour styles: "affiliative" humour brings people together, while "aggressive" humour puts others down. The first is linked with better relationships.
dropIn.source: Martin et al., "Individual differences in uses of humor…", Journal of Research in Personality (2003)
dropIn.prompt: A friend's teasing is getting mean. He shrugs: "What's the problem? It's all jokes."

options.text: It's all fine. People are too sensitive these days.
Not all jokes are the same — there's humour that brings people together and humour that puts people down. Tease the situation, not the person.
options.why: A clear, friendly rule backed by research.

options.text: Psychologists say there are different humour styles. Some humour is affiliative and some is aggressive, and they have different effects on relationships over time.
options.why: Correct but full of jargon, and it never tells him what to do.

dropIn.pattern: Turn a fact into a rule

wordPower.sentence: You're very good at avoiding work.

options.why: Fake praise for a bad habit — perfect banter.
Correct but formal. The joke loses its punch.

wordPower.example: He's a master at arriving just after the bill is paid.

options.why: Very British and a bit strong.

wordPower.meaning: Saying silly things that aren't true or don't make sense.
wordPower.example: You're talking nonsense — the bus is never early.

wordPower.sentence: After winning, he was very proud of himself.

options.why: Everyday English, perfect for friendly teasing.
Too strong and formal; it sounds like a real insult.

wordPower.example: Don't get full of yourself — it was one lucky shot.

options.why: Simple and funny when said with a smile.

wordPower.example: Your jokes are terrible, and I love them.

options.why: Formal. Sounds like a job review.
Natural, slightly teasing, easy to understand.

wordPower.meaning: Very confident, sometimes a little too much.
wordPower.example: For someone who got lost twice, you're very sure of yourself.

wordPower.sentence: Don't be angry — I was joking.
wordPower.meaning: Making fun of someone in a friendly way.
wordPower.example: I was only teasing — your Nepali is great.

options.why: Correct but very formal. It kills the banter.

wordPower.meaning: Only because of luck, not skill.
wordPower.example: You found the café by pure luck and you know it.

options.why: Sounds like a lawyer, and it's too harsh for a friend.

wordPower.example: You're a real pain, but you're my favourite pain.
